sections.h2: What should a seller know about Bulloch County, Georgia?
sections.html:
Bulloch County is a university county in southeast Georgia. Statesboro is the seat, and Georgia Southern University and East Georgia State College's Statesboro campus are both there, with Ogeechee Technical College in an unincorporated part of the county (Wikipedia). The county was created on February 8, 1796, covers about 673 square miles of land and is mostly flat coastal plain.

The 2020 census counted 81,099 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 86,949. The median age in 2020 was 28.9, and renters occupied 50.1 percent of occupied homes. For 2020 to 2024, Census QuickFacts lists a median owner-occupied value of $222,500, an owner-occupied rate of 53.1 percent and 1,389 building permits in 2025.

That mix makes Bulloch a county of student rentals, investor-owned houses and family homes. Sellers often own a rental or an inherited house, and the tax questions below apply to both.

sections.h2: Which Bulloch County offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
The county's government offices keep weekday hours of 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., according to the county website. Bulloch splits the work in a way that differs from most Georgia counties. The tax assessors, not the tax commissioner, receive tax returns and homestead applications.

Bulloch County property tax contacts, from the county's assessor, tax commissioner and payment pages

The commissioner lists propertytax@bullochcounty.net for tax questions. The county's online tax record search and payment portal are linked from the tax commissioner page. Card payments carry a convenience fee charged by the processor, not by the county.

sections.h2: How does Bulloch County value property and take returns?
sections.html:
Fair market value is set as of January 1, and the tax is levied on an assessed value that is 40 percent of it. One mill equals one dollar for each thousand dollars of assessed value. The county commissioners set the county rate, and the school board sets its own, as the assessors' page explains.

Owners must file at least an initial return for real and personal property held on January 1. In Bulloch the filing period runs from January 1 through April 1, and the return is filed with the assessors. After the first return it renews automatically at the value last finalized, and you file a new one only when you add property, make improvements or want to declare a different value.

The assessors do not take returns by email. Faxed returns must be in the office by 5:00 p.m. on the last day of the appeal period, and the board cannot waive penalties or extend a deadline.

The county held its millage rate hearings in August 2026, and the presentation is posted on the county home page.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Bulloch County assessment?
sections.html:
Appeal in writing within 45 days of the date on the notice of change. The assessors will not accept an appeal by email, and a faxed appeal must arrive by 5:00 p.m. on the final day.

The path runs through four steps:

  • The appeal is filed with the Board of Tax Assessors, which reviews it and replies.
  • If the board changes nothing, the appeal goes to the County Board of Equalization, which holds a hearing.
  • You may choose arbitration instead of the Board of Equalization when you file.
  • A taxpayer still unhappy after that may go to Superior Court.

You can appeal taxability, value or the uniformity of the value against similar properties. You cannot appeal the amount of tax levied, because that follows from the millage rate. The county also lists "Appeal for Property Tax Assessment" in its How Do I section.

sections.h2: Which Bulloch County exemptions can lower the bill?
sections.html:
The assessors list several homestead exemptions. All require that you own and occupy the home as your legal residence on January 1, and the application window is January 1 through April 1. Once granted, an exemption renews each year unless ownership changes.

  • Standard homestead: $2,000 deducted from the 40 percent assessed value.
  • Age 65 or older: $4,000 off state and county taxes, if household income is within the limit the page states.
  • Age 62 or older: a school tax exemption of up to $10,000 of assessed value, also with an income limit.
  • Disabled veterans and surviving spouses of service members: larger exemptions set by state law.

Georgia also offers a tax deferral for homeowners 62 and older who meet an income test. The tax is generally deferred until the property changes hands or the deferred amount reaches 85 percent of the property's value, so a sale triggers repayment.

Farm owners can apply for a conservation use covenant by April 1. It lasts ten years, carries a $10 recording fee and brings a penalty of twice the taxes saved if broken, so ask the assessors before you sell covenanted land.

sections.h2: How do rentals, schools and roads shape a Bulloch County sale?
sections.html:
The 2020 census recorded 32,983 housing units in Bulloch, of which 9.8 percent were vacant. The rental vacancy rate was 9.0 percent and the homeowner vacancy rate 1.4 percent. Median gross rent for 2020 to 2024 is $995, and median owner costs with a mortgage are $1,462 a month. A landlord selling a rental in Statesboro is competing for buyers in a county where about half of occupied homes were renter-occupied in 2020.

Public schools come from a single countywide district, the Bulloch County School District, and one charter school, Statesboro STEAM Academy, is chartered through a separate district. Buyers with children will ask about the school zone, and buyers who commute will ask about I-16, US 301, US 80 and US 25, which all cross the county.

  • Student rentals near the university are priced and bought differently from family homes.
  • Rural parcels outside Statesboro often come with agricultural or timber use, so ask the assessors about covenants before you list.
  • Timber harvests are handled through a separate county page, so check it if you cut trees before selling.

For any parcel, pull the tax record online first. The county's tax record search shows what the assessors have on file, and it is the quickest way to spot a wrong acreage or missing exemption.

sections.h2: Do Bulloch County cities send their own tax bills?
sections.html:
Yes for four of them. Statesboro, Brooklet, Portal and Register bill and collect real and personal property tax separately, so a house inside those limits gets one bill from the county and another from the city.

That matters at closing. A payoff request should cover both bills, and the title company needs to know which city, if any, your parcel lies in.

When you sell, ask the commissioner for a payoff and ask your closing attorney how the current year will be divided, since the due date for your bill is printed on the bill itself. If you have rental units, confirm that the owner name on the bill matches the name on the deed before the closing date.

faqs.q: Who takes homestead applications in Bulloch County?
faqs.a: The Tax Assessors office, at 113 North Main Street in Statesboro. Applications run from January 1 through April 1, and an exemption renews automatically once granted.

faqs.q: How many days do I have to appeal in Bulloch County?
faqs.a: You have 45 days from the date on the notice. The appeal must be in writing, and the assessors do not accept it by email.

faqs.q: Do Statesboro homeowners get one tax bill or two?
faqs.a: Two. Statesboro bills and collects its own real and personal property tax, so you receive a county bill and a city bill each year.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Bulloch County property tax?
faqs.a: Pay the Tax Commissioner at 113 North Main Street, Suite 101, Statesboro, or online through the county's tax payment link. Call 912-764-6285 with questions. Card payments carry a processor convenience fee.

faqs.q: Can the Bulloch County assessors waive a late filing penalty?
faqs.a: No. The assessors state that they have no authority to relieve penalties or grant extensions for filing, so submit forms by the stated deadlines.
